newsitem.title: UK: BBC World Service may launch 24 hour news service.
newsitem.headline: BBC World Service may launch 24 hour news service.

text.p: The BBC unveiled plans on Tuesday for a 24-hour global English language radio news service to complement its existing World Service output.
"The World Service has developed a detailed strategy for the next five years, for discussion with government," the BBC said in its 1996/97 annual report.
"The strategy envisages a continuous news and information service in English to be delivered alongside the existing broad mix of English language programmes," it added.
BBC director-general John Birt said the World Service was also exploring the launch of "major new services for the Internet".

Birt urged the new Labour government to adopt a "realistic" approach to funding the World Service. Under the previous government, Britain's Foreign Office last year reversed plans to cut World Service funding by five million pounds ($8.4 million).

World Service's global audience increased last year to 143 million weekly listeners from 140 million. The radio service broadcasts in 45 languages and has listeners in some 140 countries around the globe.

The BBC, which fund its domestic services through a licence fee levy on all households with a television set, said it now had a cash surplus of 365 million pounds after wiping out its borrowings in recent years.
The state-owned corporation has transformed its finances in the 1990s through cost savings and the sale of its transmission network to a U.S.-led consortium for 244 million pounds earlier this year.
Birt said that the BBC had said itself the target of boosting efficiency by a further 20 percent over the next five years.

The BBC shed 1,700 domestic staff in 1996/97 -- some eight percent of the total. Birt refused to be drawn on further job cuts but said the proportion of BBC staff involved in programme making would continue to rise.

Birt has come under fire from trades union leaders in recent days after it emerged that his salary rose almost 20 percent to 354,000 pounds last year. The BBC said the figure was broadly in line with the industry average.
The BBC plans new free services including a 24-hour television news channel next year as Britain introduces digital broadcasting, with its extra channel capacity.
The BBC has also joined forces with pay television company Flextech Plc to launch subscription channels based on the BBC's extensive programme library.

That deal has been concluded by BBC Worldwide -- the corporation's commercial arm. Worldwide contributed 73.5 million pounds to the BBC's budget in 1996/97 -- a tiny figure compared to licence fee income of more than 1.9 billion pounds.
But the BBC said Worldwide was on target to treble its contribution over the next decade.($ = 0.594 British Pounds)
